case_study_insert.main_stem: Keyline Express Transport (KET) is a private limited company in the express courier and parcel delivery sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2015 by Marcus Bell, it serves online retailers nationwide and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. KET plans to invest $1,000,000 in an automated parcel-sorting hub, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $400,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $8 a unit and a selling price of $14, and currently produces 120,000 units a year, each unit one sorted parcel. KET faces rising customer complaints about late deliveries and an absenteeism rate of 8% among warehouse staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Service Report — Q3 2025: The hub sorted 30,000 parcels last quarter with a mis-sort rate of 2.9%, down from 4.4% a year earlier. Customer complaints about late delivery rose from 51 to 73 per month. Average delivery time is 2.3 days. A survey of 600 online retailers found that 66% would pay $0.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery, and 58% rate on-time delivery as their top priority. An HR audit shows absenteeism of 8% and that 16 of 80 warehouse staff lack training on the new sorters; courses cost $560 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Keyline Express Transport for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, affecting KET's $600,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.0% from $12.00 to $12.84 per hour from April 2026. (3) Fuel and packaging input costs have risen 10.0%, while e-commerce parcel volumes grew 8.0% and the average delivery price fell 1.0%.

questions.question_text: KET financed its $1,000,000 sorting hub with a $600,000 bank loan and a $400,000 overdraft. Explain two advantages for KET of using the overdraft rather than more bank borrowing for short-term funds.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $400,000 overdraft can be drawn and repaid as needed, so KET only pays interest on the amount actually used, unlike a $600,000 bank loan that charges interest on the full sum from day one. This flexibility protects cash flow while the business carries fixed costs of $480,000 a year and faces rising late-delivery complaints, letting it cover temporary costs without raising the $14 delivery price.

Point 2: An overdraft is quicker and easier to arrange than negotiating additional term debt, so founder Marcus Bell can respond fast to the 8% absenteeism problem or to the 16 staff needing training at $560 each. It also avoids the long-term repayment commitment of a larger loan, keeping the $1,000,000 hub project from becoming a burden if e-commerce volumes shift, while preserving the $6 contribution on each of 120,000 parcels.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to KET, its financing mix and its short-term cash needs.

questions.question_text: KET is promoting its guaranteed next-day delivery service to online retailers. Consider social media influencer advertising, in-app promotions with online retailers, or local radio adverts. Which should KET choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Social media influencer advertising: Influencers could demonstrate fast parcel delivery to a broad audience at moderate cost, and campaigns are measurable through clicks. However, KET's customers are 600 surveyed online retailers rather than individual consumers, so much of the audience would never place a business contract, and the 58% who rank on-time delivery first need evidence of reliability, not lifestyle promotion.

In-app promotions with online retailers: Placing the next-day offer inside retailers' own checkout pages reaches sellers exactly when they choose a courier, and the $0.50 surcharge that 66% of 600 retailers would accept can be shown at that moment. It also addresses the 58% who prioritise on-time delivery by displaying KET's 2.3-day average and falling 2.9% mis-sort rate. The drawback is that KET must negotiate access and may pay fees to the retailers, and it depends on their platforms.

Local radio adverts: Radio is cheap and can build regional awareness of KET's service, useful given rising complaints about late deliveries. Yet KET serves online retailers nationwide, so a local audience is too narrow to fill 120,000 parcels a year, and radio cannot demonstrate the reliability that 58% of buyers demand.

Recommendation: KET should choose in-app promotions with online retailers, supported by limited social media. In-app promotions reach the actual 600 decision-makers at the point of sale and convert the finding that 66% would pay $0.50 more into revenue, while showing the reliability that 58% value. Influencer advertising is rejected as consumer-focused and weak for business contracts; local radio is rejected as too narrow for a nationwide courier serving 120,000 parcels a year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to KET.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KET with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of KET with a well-justified recommendation explaining why influencer advertising and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: KET has 8% absenteeism and 16 of 80 warehouse staff untrained on the new sorters. Explain two benefits for KET of introducing team working to improve motivation and reduce absenteeism.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working gives the 80 warehouse staff shared responsibility for sorting the 30,000 parcels each quarter, so the 8% absenteeism problem is addressed through peer support and a sense of belonging rather than top-down pressure. Teams can cover for absent colleagues, protecting the 2.3-day average delivery time and helping reduce the 73 monthly late-delivery complaints.

Point 2: Team working lets the 16 untrained staff learn from experienced colleagues on the new automated sorters, spreading skills alongside the $560 courses and reducing the 2.9% mis-sort rate. Greater involvement suits KET's flat structure and democratic leadership, raising commitment so that the $1,000,000 hub investment achieves the 1,500 parcels-per-worker productivity needed to justify the $600,000 loan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KET's absenteeism, training and service quality.

questions.question_text: KET must train 16 warehouse staff on the new automated sorters. Consider on-the-job training or external courses at $560 per employee. Which should KET choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on KET's own sorters teaches the 16 staff the exact procedures needed to cut the 2.9% mis-sort rate, costs no fees and keeps them sorting parcels while they learn, protecting the 30,000-parcel quarterly throughput. It helps address the 73 late-delivery complaints immediately. Its weaknesses are that trainer time is lost, bad habits can spread, and there is no certificate to demonstrate competence to the 600 retailers who rank on-time delivery first.

External courses at $560 per employee: These provide structured skills and a recognised qualification for all 16 staff (16 × $560 = $8,960), a small sum against the $1,000,000 hub. They take staff away from the sorter temporarily, worsening the 8% absenteeism problem in the short run, and generic content may not match KET's equipment, so follow-up on site would still be required.

Decision: KET should choose on-the-job training, with short external certification later for the most senior operators. On-the-job training is chosen because the 2.9% mis-sort rate and 73 complaints need an immediate line-specific fix, and taking 16 people away would strain the 120,000-parcel target while absenteeism is already 8%. External courses alone are rejected because $8,960 of fees plus lost sorting time would disrupt service to retailers, 58% of whom prioritise on-time delivery; certification can be added once the hub is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KET.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of KET.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of KET with a well-justified decision covering cost, service quality and output continuity.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KET's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($14 − $8) = $480,000 ÷ $6 = 80,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 80,000 parcels a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14 − $8 = $6. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KET's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. KET can compare the 80,000-parcel break-even with 120,000 parcels actually sorted, a margin of safety of 40,000 parcels, to judge whether the $1,000,000 hub is justified.
2. Contribution of $6 per parcel lets managers evaluate the $0.50 next-day surcharge that 66% of retailers would accept, and model how fuel and packaging inflation affects the $8 variable cost.
3. Fixed costs of $480,000 and $6 contribution set the 80,000-parcel minimum needed to cover costs and service the $600,000 bank loan and $400,000 overdraft.
4. Labour productivity of 120,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 1,500 parcels per worker can be tracked to judge whether the 16 trained staff and falling 2.9% mis-sort rate are improving efficiency.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 80,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 120,000-parcel output; valuing the $0.50 next-day surcharge; loan and overdraft service volume; and productivity benchmarking at 1,500 parcels per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KET's profitability using the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has KET's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $1,500,000 to $1,800,000 while cost of sales increased from $900,000 to $1,008,000; gross profit therefore rose from $600,000 to $792,000. Dividing gross profit by revenue gives 40.0% in 2024 and 44.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $180,000 on $1,500,000 and $270,000 on $1,800,000 produces 12.0% and 15.0%. Operating profit against capital employed of $1,200,000 and $1,500,000 gives 15.0% and 18.0%.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The gross margin rising from 40.0% to 44.0% shows KET kept more of each delivery fee after direct costs, supported by the $6 contribution on each parcel. The operating margin improving from 12.0% to 15.0% indicates the $480,000 fixed costs of the hub were absorbed better. Returns on capital rose from 15.0% to 18.0%, suggesting the $1,000,000 investment is adding value. However, interest payable rose from $20,000 to $25,000 as borrowing grows, and the 73 monthly late-delivery complaints plus 10.0% fuel and packaging inflation could undermine the margins if volumes fall.

Conclusion: KET's financial performance has improved. Gross margin, operating margin and returns on capital all rose, and cost of sales grew more slowly than revenue, so the improvement is real. The residual risks are rising interest and service complaints, so KET should use the improved position to fix the 8% absenteeism and protect the $0.50 premium service before margins are eroded.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether KET's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KET of introducing the guaranteed next-day delivery premium promoted in its market research.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 600 online retailers found that 66% would pay $0.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery and 58% prioritise on-time delivery, so the premium can raise revenue per parcel and protect the $6 contribution as fuel and packaging costs rise 10.0%. It also helps address the 73 monthly late-delivery complaints by giving customers a clear service promise.

Disadvantage: Guaranteeing next-day delivery raises operational risk: the current 2.3-day average and 8% absenteeism mean KET may miss promises, causing refunds and damage to relationships with the 58% who value reliability most. Extra resources needed to meet the guarantee could push up the $480,000 fixed costs or the $8 variable cost, squeezing margins if fewer than the 66% of retailers accept the $0.50 premium.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KET's survey data, service reliability and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.0% rise in fuel and packaging costs will affect KET. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If KET's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the rise is 0.75 percentage points (5.25% − 4.5%), so extra annual interest is 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year. That is small against fixed costs of $480,000 and can be removed entirely by fixing the loan rate. Higher base rates may slow consumer spending, but parcel volumes are still forecast to grow 8.0%.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, to $12.84 per hour): With a workforce of 80, warehouse and driving roles are largely hourly-paid, so the rise raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so a total cannot be honestly invented; the defensible test is productivity of 120,000 parcels ÷ 80 staff = 1,500 parcels per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable, but with 8% absenteeism and 16 untrained staff the $6 contribution per parcel could be squeezed.

Fuel and packaging costs (10.0% rise): These feed the $8 variable cost on every one of 120,000 parcels. The insert does not split that cost, so only a bound can be shown: if all $8 were affected, 10.0% × $8 = $0.80 per parcel, which at 120,000 parcels is about $96,000 a year — but fuel and packaging are only part of variable cost, so the true figure is lower and cannot be stated from the insert. With the average delivery price falling 1.0%, KET cannot easily pass this on despite the $0.50 premium that 66% would accept.

Conclusion: The 10.0% rise in fuel and packaging costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every parcel, dwarfs the $4,500 interest effect, and is harder to offset than wages because the average price is falling 1.0%. The interest rise is the smallest and hedgeable; the wage rise is serious but manageable at 1,500 parcels per worker if absenteeism is tackled. Input inflation directly attacks the $8 variable cost behind the $6 contribution, so it matters most.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to KET.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KET's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KET with a well-justified judgment that fuel and packaging inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
